prize_parts.citation: For showing that liquid-liquid phase separation and multivalent molecular interactions organise the interior of living cells into biomolecular condensates

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensates replaced a vague picture of cellular compartments with a general physical-chemical principle, phase separation driven by weak multivalent interactions. The principle is simple, has been reproduced in many independent laboratories over roughly fifteen years, and has changed how chemists and biologists treat intracellular organisation, protein self-assembly, aggregation (including amyloid) and the design of molecular interactions. It is a new concept of molecular organisation rather than a new tool. Hyman and Brangwynne gave the founding demonstration with P granules, and Rosen supplied the quantitative multivalency framework that turns the observation into chemistry. After hearing colleagues, I still rank this first, but I recognise that it has less opening support than degraders or base editing, and I would accept it as a shared-prize part if the Committee wants a two-achievement configuration.
statement.case_against: The in vivo interpretation is still contested: liquid-like behaviour does not always prove functional phase separation, and overexpression artefacts and the equilibrium-thermodynamics framing are debated. A three-name cut also omits Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and sticker-spacer work is part of the physical framework, and a strict reading of maturity could favour candidates with settled mechanisms and large demonstrated consequences, such as ionizable lipid nanoparticles, targeted degradation or base editing. Only three of eight members ranked it at all, and one placed it eighth, which signals real doubt about its chemical rather than cell-biological identity.

responses.point: Aili ranks PROTACs and molecular glues first as a designable chemical modality that makes undruggable proteins addressable, and notes that credit among Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli is plausible but crowded. He also ranks phase separation fourth and says it resonates with peptide self-assembly.
responses.response: I agree that B007 is a strong, original chemical concept and I keep it as my first alternative. Where I qualify his view is attribution and timing: the PROTAC strand (Crews, Deshaies, Sakamoto) and the cereblon or glue strand (Handa, Ito) are separate discoveries, so a three-name prize risks either splitting them awkwardly or omitting Ciulli or Handa, and no degrader has yet reached approval-level proof. I am glad he sees the overlap with self-assembly, because that is why I think condensates are chemistry and not only cell biology.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks base editing first as a conceptually simple chemical idea with a clean single-laureate story around Liu, and calls it a game-changer. He ranks degraders fourth and notes eight credited names.
responses.response: Base editing is a good chemical invention and the attribution to Liu is cleaner than for most candidates, which I accept. My reservation is context: it follows the 2020 CRISPR prize closely and its clinical durability is still being established, so I see it as the more incremental step for the Academy. A condensate prize offers a new conceptual framework in physical chemistry rather than an additional application of a recently recognised platform, and I would weigh that when comparing the two.

responses.point: Linke ranks massively parallel sequencing first as a surface and single-molecule chemistry idea that cut the cost of reading DNA by orders of magnitude and can be explained to a broad audience. He ranks phase separation eighth.
responses.response: I accept that sequencing is overdue and its impact is not in doubt, and the Balasubramanian-Klenerman reversible-terminator chemistry is real chemistry. My disagreement is that the strongest case is for technology and consequences, whereas the Prize is also for new concepts, and the 454 and Solexa lineages plus Ju and Mayer make a three-name allocation contestable. I would like him to say why he places condensates as low as eighth: if the objection is that the in vivo evidence is not yet clean enough, that is a fair maturity concern, but if it is that the field belongs to cell biology, I would argue the central ideas are thermodynamic.

responses.point: Chabes ranks degraders first, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, because ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis becomes a designable chemical reaction, and ranks base editing second as nucleobase chemistry made into a general tool.
responses.response: His argument for B007 is persuasive on originality and on the structural understanding of ternary complexes, and I think the Handa credit is important because the thalidomide-cereblon mechanism explains the glue branch. I would still ask whether the Committee prefers a prize built around PROTACs alone, which leaves Ciulli out, or a combined one, which is crowded at three names. That unresolved attribution is a reason why I do not move degraders above condensates.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee regards in vivo liquid-liquid phase separation as sufficiently settled, or only the in vitro and conceptual framework
How to allocate credit among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag within three names
Whether a two-achievement configuration, for example one degrader part and one condensate part, would be preferable but is constrained by the three-person limit
I rely on my own recollection of the literature and have not independently verified priority claims
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I share Lund University with committee colleagues Linke and Somfai, and my research on lipid-protein co-assembly and amyloid is topically close to condensates, but I have no known personal or institutional tie to Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu or Mittag.
